justice: Spatial resources are predominantly allocated to motor vehicles: a wide two-lane carriageway with centerline/edge markings is present, while no dedicated sidewalk is visible along either side.

Accessibility is limited for many users because the road edge transitions directly to a narrow grass/soil verge; this creates an uneven, unpaved walking surface that is difficult for strollers, luggage, or anyone needing stable footing.

Rules appear generally non-discriminatory (clear lane markings and a predictable roadway layout), but the lack of marked pedestrian space and crossing facilities effectively disadvantages non-drivers in practice.
safety: Vehicle guidance is relatively clear due to the centerline and solid edge lines, which can reduce head-on/edge-drift conflicts on this rural segment.
A parked truck on the right shoulder/verge creates a roadside obstacle and potential sudden merging/door-opening conflict for passing vehicles and any cyclists using the edge.

There are no visible crosswalks, pedestrian refuge areas, or speed-calming features; combined with a long straight sightline, this can encourage higher speeds and increase crash severity risk for all users.
livability: The corridor reads as low-activity and destination-poor: there are no visible storefronts, community facilities, or active frontages along the road segment.
No public amenities are apparent (e.g., benches, shelters, drinking fountains), limiting usability for lingering, waiting, or social interaction.
Green fields and low-density housing in the distance provide openness, but the environment functions mainly as a travel corridor rather than a place to stay.
sustainability: Extensive roadside greenery/vegetation and planted areas contribute to ecosystem presence and potential habitat value along the corridor.

The setting appears relatively supportive of low-emission travel in principle (open shoulders and low congestion), but the absence of dedicated walking/cycling infrastructure reduces practical mode shift away from cars.
No visible stormwater management features (e.g., bioswales, permeable sidewalks) are evident; drainage appears to rely on vegetated verges/ditches rather than designed green infrastructure.
aesthetics: The landscape has strong visual openness with green fields, scattered trees, and distant hillside/settlement, creating a pleasant rural scenic quality.
Streetlights and orderly roadway markings provide a neat, coherent linear streetscape.
Aesthetics are weakened by the utilitarian roadside condition (unpaved verges/shoulders and a parked truck dominating the right edge), which reduces visual refinement.
comfort: Thermal comfort is mixed: there is abundant vegetation, but limited continuous tree canopy over the roadway/verge, offering little shade for people walking or cycling along the edge.
Physical comfort for non-motorized users is low because the road margin appears to be grass/soil rather than smooth, level paving; this increases fatigue and reduces perceived stability.
Psychological comfort is moderate: the road feels open and uncrowded, but the lack of separation from moving traffic (no sidewalk/buffer) can make walking/cycling feel exposed.
walkability: No continuous sidewalk is visible; pedestrians would likely have to use the narrow grass/soil verge along the right side or the road edge line, reducing safety and comfort.
There are no marked pedestrian crossings or traffic-calming elements to support safe crossing or walking in both directions along this corridor.
While the roadway surface is smooth, the pedestrian realm is discontinuous and informal (verge-only), limiting accessibility and making longer walks unattractive for most users.
bikeability: There is no dedicated bike lane or protected cycling facility; cyclists would need to share the travel lane or ride near the edge line/shoulder.
The parked truck on the right side creates a pinch point and forces cyclists to merge into the motor-vehicle lane, increasing conflict risk.
The long, straight alignment and clear lane markings can aid predictability, but the lack of buffering from traffic and unclear shoulder quality reduce overall cycling comfort.
